title: Agency Information Collection Activities; Submission to the Office of Management and Budget for Review and Approval; Comment Request; Requirements for Patent Applications Containing Nucleotide Sequence and/or Amino Acid Sequence Disclosures
summary:
The latest Federal Register highlights three government updates: the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office is seeking final public comments on its rules for including DNA and protein sequence listings in patent applications, the postal regulator is reviewing new and amended shipping contracts from the Postal Service and inviting feedback, and the Department of Veterans Affairs is announcing members of its executive performance review board.

For inventors and biotech companies, the patent notice matters because it keeps the rules clear for how sequence data must be submitted. Examiners rely on these listings to judge what’s new and what’s not, and applicants use them to describe their inventions. The agency estimates about 30,000 filings a year and roughly six hours of work per submission, plus some out-of-pocket costs. The upside is predictability and smoother examination; the downside is time and expense, which can weigh more heavily on small teams and startups. Comments are open until November 24, 2025, at reginfo.gov.

On shipping, the Postal Regulatory Commission is signaling that the Postal Service has filed several custom contract requests, including an amendment to an existing package deal and a new Priority Mail contract. Some standardized contract types are also moving forward through a quicker review. This could benefit high-volume shippers that qualify for tailored pricing or service options, and potentially consumers if efficiencies lead to better offerings. Others—especially businesses that don’t qualify for special terms—may worry about uneven access to lower rates or limited transparency when certain requests skip public comment. Feedback on the public items is due October 29, 2025, at prc.gov.

The Veterans Affairs notice is a routine step to name members of its Performance Review Board, which helps ensure senior leaders are evaluated fairly. This supports accountability and stable management. It has little direct effect on most readers but contributes to oversight of a large public service agency.

Overall, these notices aim to balance transparency and efficiency. The benefits are clearer rules, targeted services, and stronger governance; the trade-offs are added paperwork for some and limited input windows for others.
